title: The one who would be a steward
hookLine: Allah tells the angels He will place a steward on the earth, and they ask why (2:30)
last: JUZ' 'AMMA — THE ONES EVERY MUSLIM CHILD KNOWS.

cards: The first story doesn't start on earth at all. It starts in a conversation. God speaks to the angels, who in this verse describe themselves as hymning His praise, and tells them a plan: something new is coming.
And the angels do something surprising. They ask a question.

So begins camp two, the stories: the prophets, one after another, Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Yusuf, Maryam and Isa, and then the Prophet himself, peace be upon him, told in words only, the way the Qur'an tells them.

teach.h: I AM ABOUT TO PLACE A VICEROY.
teach.b: Here's the verse, surah two, verse thirty. God says to the angels, in Pickthall's words: “Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth.” Viceroy is Pickthall's choice.

teach.h: KHALIFAH — ONE WHO STANDS IN FOR.
teach.b: The Arabic is khalifah, and translators wrestle with it: viceroy, deputy, successor, steward. The root, kh-l-f, means to come after, to stand in for. A khalifah is someone who holds a place on another's behalf.
Not the owner. The one entrusted. The later word caliph comes from it, but here it's about every human being.

And the angels answer. Paraphrasing: will You place there someone who will spread corruption and shed blood, while we praise You and call You holy? Commentators are careful here: this was a question, not an objection.
They wanted to understand. How could something that dangerous be the one put in charge? And God doesn't strike them down for asking.

teach.h: I KNOW WHAT YOU KNOW NOT.
teach.b: He answers, in Pickthall's words: “Surely I know that which ye know not.” Tomorrow the story shows them what He meant. This first scene sets something up.
Human beings enter the story as a risk, and a trust at the same time. Capable of bloodshed. Handed the earth anyway, to look after.
And the first thing that happens, before anyone has done anything, is an honest question, asked out loud, to God, and answered.

how: Many Muslims understand being a khalifah on the earth as a trust: caring for creation and for one another as stewards answerable to God, and Friday sermons often return to this verse.

o: an angel set over the earth to record deeds
a king who owns the earth outright
a steward holding the earth on another's behalf

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.
p: to come after, to stand in for

s: in this scene the angels rebel against God
commentators stress it was a question, not a rebellion. they wanted to understand.
khalifah here refers only to a political ruler
the later title caliph comes from it, but in 2:30 it's about human beings as stewards of the earth.
"Surely I know that which ye know not."

games.q: you're one of the angels. God says He'll place a steward on the earth, one who might shed blood. what do you do?
games.why: the angels asked: will You place there someone who will shed blood? and God answered them, not in anger: I know what you know not.

practice: Let one real question come up, one you've been carrying about your life, or the world, or God: not a rhetorical one, but the kind you'd feel a little shy asking out loud, in plain words.

Just sit with it; you don't have to answer it, and in the story, even the angels asked, and nobody was punished for it. If you pray, you can ask it there; if you don't, just hold it in the open, and let it breathe.

wordCard.voice: Khalifah. A steward, a deputy, one who stands in for another. The Qur'an's word, in this scene, for what a human being is here to be.

orig.note: Arabic: steward, deputy, successor, from kh-l-f, to come after; the source of the English word caliph.

carryVoice: Your line: even the angels asked. Camp two has begun. Day twenty-two, done.
